title: Won Buddhism
hookLine: a Korean Buddhism of the twentieth century centered on a simple circle

lines: WHAT IS IT A PICTURE OF?
cards: On the altar there's no statue. No seated figure, no gold, no face. There's a circle: a plain black ring on a white field, framed and hung where a Buddha image might be.
People bow to it, sit facing it in silence, and chant before it on a Sunday morning, in Seoul or in a converted house in an American suburb. A child in the back row might ask what it's a picture of.

teach.b: First, the beginning. Won Buddhism is a modern Korean Buddhism. Its founder is known to his followers as Sotaesan.
Tradition says he spent years searching for the truth without a teacher, questioning and struggling, until he awakened.
Afterward he read the Buddhist scriptures, recognized his own awakening in the Buddha's teaching, and founded a new community. Won is the Korean word for circle. Second, the circle.
It's called Il-Won-Sang, the One Circle image. Won Buddhists explain it as a symbol of the dharmakaya, the truth-body of the Buddha: the original nature of all beings and the source of everything.
It isn't a picture of a person. It's a picture of what is already whole, before anyone draws a line through it, which is why it stands where a statue would. Third, what follows.
If the one truth is everywhere, then, in a phrase Won Buddhists use, everywhere is a Buddha image, and every act is an offering to the Buddha.
Your coworker, your child, the person in line at the pharmacy: each is a place to meet the Buddha. Work and family aren't interruptions of practice; they're where it happens.
Won Buddhists speak of timeless Zen and placeless Zen: meditation that doesn't wait for the right hour or the right room. Fourth, the purpose.
The founder's motto, in a paraphrase: as material civilization opens up, a spiritual civilization should open up with it.
So Won Buddhism runs schools and charities alongside its temples, and its ministers, women and men alike, serve congregations that meet on ordinary weekends.

how: Won Buddhists enshrine the Il-Won-Sang, a plain circle, on their altars instead of a Buddha statue, meet for weekly services with meditation and chanting, and aim to practice anywhere and at any time, treating all things as a Buddha and every act as an offering.

games.q: you're Sotaesan, founding a new community. what do you place on the altar?
games.why: a plain circle, the One Circle image: a picture of the truth that is already whole, everywhere, not a picture of a person.

practice: If you have paper and a pen, draw one circle in a single motion, without lifting the pen, and don't fix it, even if it wobbles; with no paper, trace one slowly in the air.

Rest your eyes on it: the inside, the outside, and the line between them. Let the breath go around with it, beginning and ending in the same place, and let it stand for a few moments for something whole.

wordCard.voice: Won Buddhism. A modern Korean Buddhism founded by Sotaesan, whose altar holds a plain circle, the One Circle image of the truth that is everywhere. Today's word.

orig.note: Korean Il-Won-Sang, the One Circle image (in Chinese characters 一圓相), at the center of Won Buddhist altars.

carryVoice: Your line: the circle. Everywhere a Buddha image, and every act an offering. Until tomorrow.
